name: Centella asiatica

card.summary: Gotu kola, the 'cica' plant behind many calming Korean skincare products; trials on wound and scar healing exist, but evidence for anti-aging or looks is small and mixed in quality.
card.aka: Cica, tiger grass, gotu kola, Indian pennywort, madecassoside, asiaticoside
card.note: Evidence is mainly wound healing, small trials and lab studies; cosmetic claims rest on limited human data.

quick.overview:
Centella asiatica is a creeping plant used for centuries in Ayurvedic and traditional Chinese medicine and now widely used in skincare as 'cica'. Its active compounds are triterpenes such as asiaticoside, madecassoside, asiatic acid and madecassic acid.

Reviews describe benefits for wound healing and scars, and there are small trials in aging skin and post-procedure recovery. Large, long trials on cosmetic outcomes are lacking in the published literature, and forums rarely discuss it for appearance.
quick.mechanism: In cell and animal studies, the triterpenes stimulate collagen I and growth factors involved in repair and reduce inflammatory markers such as IL-1 beta and IL-6. A systematic review of four clinical trials suggested it might enhance wound healing through improved angiogenesis.
quick.risks: The published literature give little safety detail; labels for topical or oral products carry the usual precautions. Oral use appears in trials in diabetes and cognition, which are outside appearance use. Dermatology reviews recommend further research on safety, dosing and standardisation.

lead: Centella asiatica (gotu kola, Indian pennywort) is a creeping herb of the Apiaceae family used for centuries in Ayurvedic and traditional Chinese medicine and as a leafy vegetable in parts of South and Southeast Asia.[1][14][31] Its principal active compounds are pentacyclic triterpenes: asiaticoside, madecassoside, asiatic acid and madecassic acid.[2][4]

In skincare it is the best-known soothing botanical, sold in creams, serums, sheet masks and ampoules (often marketed as "cica"). People use it to calm redness and irritation, support recovery after procedures, soften the look of scars and stretch marks and, in anti-aging products, to support firmer-looking skin.[4][12] The appearance chain runs from collagen and wound-healing activity to calmer, more even-looking skin.[6][2]

A 2022 systematic review of four clinical trials concluded that it might enhance wound healing, while noting the small evidence base.[6] For cosmetic outcomes such as wrinkles, skin quality or looks, published work consists of small studies; a 2024 review of cosmeceuticals for photoaging included it among botanical agents.[3][8][11]

paras: Centella asiatica is a perennial herb with creeping stolons, long-stalked green leaves and tiny white or crimson flowers that sit in small clusters near the soil surface; its densely reticulate fruit distinguishes it from Hydrocotyle species.[31] It is native to tropical regions of Africa, Asia, Australia and western Pacific islands, grows in swampy areas, and is considered invasive on several Pacific islands.[31] Regional names include vallaarai in Sri Lanka, pegaga in Malay and Thankuni Pata in Bangladesh and West Bengal.[31]

As food, the leaves are eaten in Sri Lanka as a green called gotu kola or vallaarai, often as malluma with rice, and in Indonesia in salads and asinan.[31] About 124 compounds have been identified in the plant, including pentacyclic triterpenoids and their glycosides, centellose and centelloside.[31]

Reviews of Centella asiatica in cosmetology and dermatology describe its use for wound healing, scars, burns, psoriasis and skin aging in topical products [4][2]. A 2025 clinical trial examined a cream in aging skin [8], and a registered study examined an extracellular-vesicle-based Centella formulation for skin quality, wrinkles and pigmentation [21]. A 2025 split-face trial tested a facial mask containing soothing ingredients for skin recovery after photorejuvenation [10], and a registered pilot tested topical Centella on the appearance of stretch marks [25].
A 2026 randomized trial examined oral Centella asiatica extract on skin-aging parameters in middle-aged Korean women [11].

Clinical trials include topical cream for scar tenderness after carpal tunnel surgery [19], herbal extracts added to silicone gel for sternotomy scars [9], oral extract for glycemic and lipid control in type 2 diabetes [7], and standardised triterpenes for diabetic neuropathy [22]. Early trials examine pharmacokinetics and safety in cognitive impairment and in older adults [20][24][26][18]. Dental trials have studied toothpaste and mouthwash containing it [17][23].

In a classic animal study, topical asiaticoside increased hydroxyproline, tensile strength and collagen content in guinea pig wounds and improved healing in diabetic rats [15]. Cell studies show that asiatic acid inhibits inflammatory mediators in macrophages [16]. A 2022 systematic review links its effects to stimulation of collagen I, fibroblast growth factor and vascular endothelial growth factor production, and to reduced IL-1 beta, IL-6 and tumour necrosis factor, although this rests on four trials [6]. A 2026 article reports that madecassoside improved wound healing in an experimental model and protected keratinocytes against UVB damage [13]. A 2023 review summarises the pharmacological activities of asiaticoside and madecassoside [5].
Traditional systems use the plant for skin conditions and minor wounds, which is the origin of its modern wound-healing and cosmetic research.[14][31]

Centella asiatica has long been used in folk medicine across Asia and Africa for skin conditions and minor wounds, and a review of the plant's pharmacology describes it as used as a 'panacea' for around three thousand years.[4][31] In Ayurveda and traditional Chinese medicine it is associated with memory and brain function as well as wound care, and asiaticoside and madecassoside are the marker compounds of the plant in the Chinese Pharmacopoeia.[5]

As a food, it appears in Burmese salads, Sri Lankan leaf dishes, Indonesian and Malay salads, Thai and Vietnamese drinks and Bengali snacks.[31] The plant takes up heavy metals from soil, a property noted in the Wikipedia article as relevant to phytoremediation.[31]

sections.h: How it is used for appearance
paras: In cosmetic products the extract or its isolated triterpenes are formulated into creams, serums, toners, sheet masks and balms, usually for sensitive, irritated or post-procedure skin. Reviews describe uses for small wounds, hypertrophic scars and keloids, burns, striae (stretch marks), cellulite and photoaged skin.[2][4][14] The proposed appearance chain is that the triterpenes support fibroblast activity and collagen synthesis while dampening inflammation, so skin looks calmer and scars look flatter and more even.[2][6]

Cosmetic reviews note the triterpenes are also formulated into anti-aging and firming products, and the plant is combined with other soothing ingredients in masks used after photorejuvenation treatments.[3][10] Oral supplements are used separately, and a 2026 trial examined an oral extract on skin-aging parameters in middle-aged Korean women.[11]

In Korean and Western skincare marketing the plant is sold under the name 'cica' and is associated with calming redness, supporting the skin barrier and aftercare for procedures. Korean cosmetics grew into a worldwide industry through the Korean wave and export by large firms such as Amorepacific and LG Household and Health Care, which is how many ingredients of the category reached international shoppers.[32]

Forum discussion of the plant is mostly outside the appearance context. T Nation members mention gotu kola in cognition and mood supplement stacks, with one user reporting it stabilised mood, and as an ingredient in blends discussed for physique.[28][29][30]

About 124 compounds have been identified, centred on pentacyclic triterpenoids: the glycosides asiaticoside and madecassoside and their aglycones asiatic acid and madecassic acid, plus centellose and centelloside.[31] Chromosome-level genome assemblies were published in 2021 and a telomere-to-telomere genome in 2025, which researchers are using to study how the plant makes its triterpenoids.[31] Reviews credit the triterpenes with wound-healing, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and antifibrotic properties in laboratory work.[14][5]

A 2022 systematic review found four clinical trials of Centella asiatica for wound healing, measuring wound contraction, healing time, pain scores and erythema, and concluded it might enhance healing [6]. A 2024 review of topical use in wound healing discusses mechanisms and clinical efficacy [12].

A 2013 review of Centella asiatica in dermatology described effects on fibroblast proliferation, collagen and fibronectin synthesis and the tensile strength of new skin, and suggested uses in photoaging, cellulite and striae, with the authors calling for clinical confirmation.[2] A 2000 review of the plant's chemical and clinical profile described it as having been subject to relatively extensive clinical investigation compared with many herbal medicines.[14]

For appearance outcomes, published studies are small: a cream in aging skin [8], an oral extract on skin aging parameters in middle-aged women [11], silicone gel with herbal extracts on post-sternotomy scars [9], and a 15-person stretch-mark appearance study [25]. A systematic review of cosmeceuticals for photoaging included Centella asiatica among botanicals, noting that evidence for cosmeceuticals ranged from Level I to II, and that peptides had the strongest evidence base [3].
No large, long-term randomized trials of Centella asiatica for wrinkles, pores or facial appearance have been published; the appearance studies above are small.

Wikipedia notes that 2024 reviews link foods and supplements containing the plant to contact dermatitis, jaundice and liver disease, with case reports of liver disease after several weeks of use; topical use can cause skin irritation and drowsiness may follow ingestion.[31] Wikipedia also states that clinical efficacy and safety of medicinal use have not been proven in clinical research.[31]

For cosmetic use, published safety information is limited. A US label for a Centella asiatica whole-plant product lists use for skin rash with flaky skin and refers to the front panel for symptoms.[27] Trials in other populations include safety endpoints, for example safety and target engagement in cognitive impairment.[20]

Posts on T Nation mention gotu kola in the context of supplement stacks for cognition or mood rather than appearance; one user describes alternating it with other supplements and reports an anxiety-reducing effect.[30][28][29] These are personal reports. In skincare communities, the plant is better known through the cica trend, where creams and masks are used for soothing and post-procedure care.[4][12]

timeline.event: Linnaeus describes the plant as Hydrocotyle asiatica; it was later reclassified into Centella by Urban (1879), according to an encyclopedic summary [1].
A study reports that topical asiaticoside improved wound healing in guinea pigs and diabetic rats [15].
A review of the East Asian medicinal plant's chemical, pharmacological and clinical profile is published [14].
Asiatic acid shown to inhibit inflammatory mediators NO and PGE2 in macrophage cells [16].
Reviews of Centella asiatica in cosmetology and in dermatology are published [4][2].
Chromosome-level genome assemblies of the plant are published [31].
A systematic review of four clinical trials concludes Centella asiatica might enhance wound healing [6].
Reviews link foods and supplements containing the plant to contact dermatitis and liver disease case reports; a review of topical use in wound healing is published [31][12].
A clinical trial of a Centella cream in aging skin is published [8].

lore.intro: Centella asiatica is discussed in skincare circles as 'cica' for calming and scars, and on supplement forums mostly for mood and cognition rather than appearance.[28][30]

claims.claim: Cica soothes redness and irritated skin.
claims.believers: Users of cica creams and masks describe calmer, less reactive skin after irritation or procedures.[4][10]
claims.experts: A split-face trial studied a mask with soothing ingredients after photorejuvenation, and laboratory work shows the triterpenes reduce inflammatory mediators.[10][16]

claims.claim: Centella helps scars and stretch marks look better.
claims.believers: Proponents say it supports collagen and flattens scars and striae.[2][4]
claims.experts: Reviews describe use for hypertrophic scars; small trials examined silicone gel with herbal extracts on sternotomy scars and a registered pilot of stretch marks. Large trials are lacking.[9][25][2]

claims.believers: Traditional systems have used it on wounds for centuries.[14][31]
claims.experts: A 2022 systematic review of four clinical trials concluded it might enhance healing, and animal work showed higher collagen and tensile strength.[6][15]

claims.claim: Centella has anti-aging effects on skin.
claims.believers: Cosmetic marketers and reviews describe firming and anti-photoaging uses.[4][3]
claims.experts: A 2025 cream trial and a 2026 oral-extract trial examined skin aging, and a photoaging review included it among botanicals.[8][11][3]

claims.claim: Gotu kola calms anxiety and sharpens memory.
claims.believers: A T Nation member reported it stabilised mood and has an anti-anxiety effect.[30]
claims.experts: Early trials examine safety and pharmacokinetics in cognitive impairment and older adults; these are not cosmetic studies.[20][24][26]

claims.claim: Gotu kola is harmless because it is a food herb.
claims.believers: The plant is eaten as a leafy vegetable in several countries.[31]
claims.experts: 2024 reviews cited by Wikipedia link supplements to contact dermatitis, jaundice and liver disease case reports.[31]

Cell and animal work shows more collagen and growth-factor signalling and less inflammation
Calmer, smoother-looking skin and less visible scarring
angle.text: Centella is used in topical products to calm irritated or recovering skin and to improve the look of scars and aging skin. Mechanism studies describe collagen stimulation and reduced inflammatory signalling; clinical studies of appearance outcomes are small.
